anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5.title: ChatGPT describes your company from five pages, so make them agree
anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5.content:
The advice that ranks for getting named by ChatGPT is mostly about formatting: put the answer in the first line, write your headers as questions, keep paragraphs short. It helps a little at the margin. A small company has a bigger lever, which is that the handful of pages describing it should say the same thing. Whatever they agree on is what an AI answer will tell people about you.

## Ask first, and write down what it says

Open ChatGPT and ask it what your company does, who it is for, what it costs and how it compares with the two competitors you think about most. Paste each answer into a document and split it into sentences, one per line. Mark each sentence true, out of date, or wrong. Don't fix anything yet. You are collecting a description you didn't write, and you need all of it on one page before you can tell which pages it came from.

Nothing about this costs money, and an hour is enough. You will probably find a sentence or two you would never say to a customer. Those are the useful ones, because each one traces back to a page somewhere.

## A small company gives the answer very little to read

Nobody outside OpenAI can tell you which pages ChatGPT used for a given answer, so this post works from an assumption. When an answer is backed by search, it behaves like the retrieval-augmented systems described in the research literature. Such a system [fetches passages from an external corpus in response to a query](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05085v5) and the model writes from what came back, which is meant to [ground its output in retrieved, verifiable information](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05085v5) instead of whatever the model half remembers. Treat that as a working model of ChatGPT, not a law about it.

Under that model, the size of your footprint matters a great deal. A large company has thousands of pages, reviews, press articles and forum threads, so one stale page is outvoted. You have a homepage, a pricing page, a LinkedIn company page, a couple of directory listings and a short run of recent posts. Each of those carries a large share of whatever the answer says.

## Whatever the pages agree on becomes your description

Agreement is the part that feels like good news, and it is, until you check what they agree on. Picture a company that pivoted from selling to freelancers to selling to agencies. The homepage was rewritten on the day of the pivot. The directory listing, the LinkedIn tagline and four of the last five posts still say "for freelancers". Three sources against one is not a close call, so the answer calls you a freelancer tool and the homepage has no say.

This is how the parts you stopped believing last year survive. Nobody decided to keep them. They sit in places you wrote once and never opened again, and the answer treats them as current because nothing contradicts them. Your own sense of the company has moved on while those pages have not, and the answer follows the pages.

Depth inside a page matters too. Engineers at LinkedIn, building a question-answering system over support tickets, found that cutting long documents into fixed-length segments [can split related content](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.17723v1), for example a ticket that describes a problem at the start and the solution at the end, and the answer comes out incomplete. A product page that makes a claim in the first paragraph and qualifies it eight hundred words later can be read the same way, with the claim retrieved and the qualification missing. Put the condition in the same paragraph as the claim.

## When two pages disagree, you don't pick the winner

Disagreement is the harder case. Say your pricing page lists a free plan and a directory listing still says "no free tier". An answer might repeat one of them. It might blur both into "pricing varies". It might name a price that appears on neither, and you can't predict which.

A question that touches several of your pages makes it worse. Take "what does it cost for a ten-person agency?" It needs the pricing page and the homepage together. ETH Zurich researchers describe queries that need several documents with substantially different contents as [common in practice and hard to serve](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05085v5), because the documents' embeddings can sit far apart and a system may not fetch all of them. If it fetches only one of your two pages, the answer is built from half the evidence.

You also can't ask the system why it chose what it chose. A Fraunhofer IAIS paper on explaining such systems starts from the observation that [the models are not intrinsically explainable](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.07620v1), which is why end users often find them less trustworthy. For you that means the audit has to happen on the pages, because the answer won't show its work.

## List your pages and mark every difference

Make a spreadsheet with one column per page and one row per claim. The pages are:

1. Your homepage.
2. Your pricing page.
3. Your LinkedIn company page.
4. Every directory or marketplace listing you can find (search your company name and see which ones appear on page one).
5. Your last five blog posts.

The rows are the things a stranger would ask. What you sell, who it is for, what it costs, what is included, when you started, how many people work there, and the name of the thing itself. Product names drift more than anything else, and "the dashboard" on one page becomes "the workspace" on another.

Fill each cell with the exact words the page uses, copied, not summarised. Then read across each row and highlight every cell that differs from the others. Differences in emphasis count. If one page leads with speed and another leads with price, an answer built from both has to choose, and it may choose the page you care about least.

The highlighted cells are your work list. Rank them by how much a prospect would care. A wrong price outranks a wrong founding year, and a wrong customer description outranks both.

## Fix your own pages first, then ask the owners of the rest

Start with the pages you can edit today, which are the homepage, the pricing page, the LinkedIn page and your own posts. Pick one wording for each claim and paste it into all of them. Decide which of the conflicting versions is true, then make the others match it. If the true answer is that you have changed your mind about who you serve, say so on the homepage in one plain sentence and delete the old audience from everywhere you control.

Old posts are the awkward case. You will be tempted to rewrite them all, and you shouldn't. Edit the ones that state something now false, and add a line at the top of any post that describes the old product, saying what changed and linking to the current page. Leave the rest alone.

Then go to the pages other people own. Directory listings usually have a "claim this profile" button or a support address, and most take a few days to update. Write a short email with the exact corrected text pasted in, so the person on the other end only has to copy it. Expect some to ignore you. For those, make sure your own pages are the loudest version of the truth and move on.

## Agreement makes the description accurate, and that is where it stops

This fixes what ChatGPT says when it already talks about you. It does not make ChatGPT bring you up in a category where nobody has written about you. If you ask for "tools for X" and the answer lists three competitors, those three are the companies that other people, in other places, have described as tools for X. Consistent pages on your own site can't supply that third-party writing. Reviews, comparisons, press mentions and mentions in other people's posts do that, and they take months.

So expect the audit to change the sentences about you. It will remove the stale audience, the wrong price and the old product name, and make a vague line more specific. It won't make you the first name in a list you aren't on, and anyone who promises otherwise for the price of reformatting your blog is guessing.

Buy an agency or a tool for that second job once the first one is done. Until the pages agree, you would pay to spread a description that contradicts itself.

## Ask again in a month and compare line by line

Ask the same questions you started with, word for word, and paste the new answers beside the old ones. Compare them sentence by sentence. Some sentences will have changed because you fixed the pages behind them. Some will not have changed, and each one points to a page you missed or to an owner who hasn't replied. Add those to the list and go around again.

Note also which competitors appear in the new answers and which don't. If you are still absent from a category list, the pages are no longer your problem. Writing about you in places you don't own is the next job.

anthropic/claude-opus-5.5.title: ChatGPT describes your company from five pages, so make them agree
anthropic/claude-opus-5.5.content:
Open ChatGPT this week and ask it what your company does. Then copy the answer into a document, one sentence per line, and date it. That transcript tells you which version of your company the internet has settled on. Most advice about AI answers tells you to format posts with direct answers and question headers. For a small company, a bigger lever sits elsewhere. The handful of pages that describe you need to say the same thing.

## Write down what ChatGPT says about you today

Ask more than once and in more than one way, because a single answer is a single draw. These four questions cover most of what a prospect would ask:

- What does [your company] do?
- Who is [your company] for?
- How much does [your company] cost?
- Which tools would you recommend for [your category]?

Put every sentence of every answer on its own line. Next to each one, write whether it is true, out of date, wrong or too vague to judge. If ChatGPT shows the pages it read, list those too, because they are the first suspects. The fourth question is the painful one. Your competitors get named with a reason attached, and you get a polite generic line or no mention at all. Keep that answer. It matters later, when we get to what this work can and can't fix.

## A small company gives the answer very little to read

OpenAI doesn't publish exactly how ChatGPT picks the pages it reads when it searches, so treat what follows as the closest public description of the mechanism, and don't mistake it for a blueprint. Researchers at ETH Zurich describe the standard design, called retrieval-augmented generation, in plain steps. The question is turned into an embedding. A search [retrieves the most relevant data items](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05085v5). Those items go to the language model, which writes the answer from them.

Now picture the pile of pages each company puts in front of that search. HubSpot has years of posts, help articles, press coverage and reviews, so any single stale page drowns in the crowd. You have a homepage, a pricing page, a LinkedIn company page, a G2 listing, maybe a Crunchbase profile and a few blog posts. Each of them carries a large share of everything the model can find about you. A team from Deloitte and NVIDIA put the consequence bluntly when they wrote that the material retrieval brings back ["determines the quality of the final output"](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.13163v2). For a big company, that sentence describes a statistical average. For you, it describes your LinkedIn About section from 2022.

## Whatever your pages agree on becomes your description

Agreement reads as fact. If four of your pages say the same thing, the answer will very likely say it too, whether or not you still believe it.

Here is how that goes wrong. Say you sold to agencies for your first two years and moved to in-house marketing teams last spring. You rewrote the homepage the week you decided. The LinkedIn company page still says agencies, and so does Crunchbase. Three blog posts from the agency era are still live, each one opening with "for agencies that...". The homepage is now outvoted four to one, and the answer tells your prospect you're an agency tool. Nobody lied. The old pages simply kept agreeing with each other after you stopped agreeing with them.

Prices drift the same way. A launch post that mentioned your old starter plan, a directory listing with last year's tiers and a comparison table on a partner's site make a fine little consensus, and it's wrong.

## When pages disagree, you don't choose which one wins

Two pages that contradict each other leave the model three options. It can repeat one of them, repeat the other, or write something soft enough to cover both. You don't get to pick, and you can't easily find out why it picked what it did. Researchers at Fraunhofer IAIS point out that the models in these systems [are not intrinsically explainable](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.07620v1), which is the reason they built tools to reconstruct what the model paid attention to.

Pages also get read in pieces. Engineers at LinkedIn found that cutting long support tickets into fixed-length chunks could separate the description of a problem from its solution, and [produce incomplete answers](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.17723v1). Your pricing page can suffer the same fate. The chunk with the plan names might travel without the chunk that says which plan includes what.

The soft answer deserves a closer look, because it's probably the one you got. "Offers flexible plans for teams of various sizes" is what a careful writer produces when two sources disagree on the numbers. We can't prove that's what happened in your case. It is the first thing worth ruling out, and ruling it out costs an afternoon.

## Audit every page that describes you

Make a list of every page a search could plausibly find when someone asks about you by name or by category. For most small companies it looks like this:

- the homepage and the About page
- the pricing page
- the LinkedIn company page and the founder's LinkedIn headline
- directory listings on G2, Capterra, Crunchbase, Product Hunt, and any directory specific to your category
- your last five blog posts
- any partner, integration or marketplace page that describes you

Open a spreadsheet with one column per page. Each row is a claim a prospect would care about: who the product is for, what it does in one sentence, the price of each plan, the plan names, what each plan includes, which integrations exist, which customers you name, where you're based and how big you are. Fill in what each page says, word for word where you can. Then mark every cell that differs from the version you'd sign today. Also mark claims that appear on only one page, because a fact with no second witness is easy for the model to drop.

Expect this to be embarrassing. The founder's LinkedIn headline usually describes the company two pivots ago, and the Capterra listing was filled in by whoever was the first hire.

## Fix your own pages first, then ask for the rest

Start with the pages you can edit tonight: the homepage, the pricing page, the blog and your LinkedIn page. Old blog posts are the awkward case. A post from the agency era can stay up if it's still useful, but add a dated line at the top that says what changed, so the post and your homepage stop contradicting each other. Where an old post states a price, correct the price or remove it.

Directory listings come next. G2, Capterra and Crunchbase all let a company claim its own profile, and once you have, the description and plans are yours to correct. Pages owned by other people (a partner's integration page, an old review, a journalist's roundup) take an email. Keep the request to one corrected sentence and a link to the current page, which makes it a two-minute job for the person reading it. Work in the order ChatGPT cited the pages when it answered you, since those are the ones it already reaches for.

## Agreeing pages won't put you on a shortlist nobody wrote you onto

Once your pages agree, the answer to "what does your company do" should get more accurate. The answer to "which tools would you recommend for your category" may not move at all. The model can only repeat a connection between your name and your category if some page makes that connection. If every page that lists tools in your category was written by someone who has never heard of you, a perfectly consistent homepage changes nothing about that list.

Getting onto the shortlist takes pages by other people that put you in the category: reviews, comparison articles, press, a customer's post about how they chose you. That work is slower, it costs more, and nobody can promise you the result, whatever the agency pitch decks say. Do the audit first anyway. If a reviewer does write about you next quarter, you want the model to read a description that matches your homepage.

## Ask again in a month and compare line by line

Put a date in your calendar four weeks out. Ask the same questions, word for word, and run each one several times, since answers vary from one run to the next. Lay the new sentences next to the old ones. Some lines will have changed to match the pages you fixed. Others will still carry the old claim, and those point to a page you missed, or one whose owner hasn't answered your email. That second list is next month's work.

openai/gpt-5.6-sol.title: ChatGPT may describe your company from the pages that agree
openai/gpt-5.6-sol.content:
Ask ChatGPT what your company does, who it serves, what it sells, and which category it belongs in. Copy the answer into a document and put every sentence on its own line.

Mark each sentence as accurate, stale, unsupported or too vague to judge. Save the prompt, the answer and the date. You will use them again after you fix the pages behind the description.

Start with contradictions before you turn every subhead into a question and every opening paragraph into a definition. Question headers and direct answers make a page tidy. They cannot reconcile a homepage that says you serve agencies with a LinkedIn page that says you built the product for in-house marketers.

## A small set of pages carries a lot of weight

When an AI system retrieves material before it answers, it selects relevant documents and gives them to the language model as context. [Researchers at Bielefeld University and Fraunhofer IAIS describe this as a retriever working with a generator](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.07620v1). The answer depends partly on which documents the retriever found and which passages the generator used.

That description covers retrieval-augmented generation in general. It does not reveal the private machinery behind any particular ChatGPT answer. Treat your result as a test of what came back, rather than a diagnosis of how the system works.

Now search for your company name in a private browser window. Ignore your knowledge of the company and look at the result as a stranger would. You may find your homepage, pricing page, LinkedIn profile, directory records and a recent article. That is your working set.

A company with little coverage gives every visible page more influence. If the homepage says one thing and an old directory listing says another, there may be little independent material available to settle the disagreement. A stale paragraph can carry far more authority than it deserves simply because there is little else to read.

## Agreement becomes the company shorthand

Imagine a company called Northstar. Its homepage describes a reporting tool for finance departments. LinkedIn still calls it project-management software for agencies. A directory listing says consultants use it to prepare client presentations. The pricing page mentions plans for freelancers.

Each statement may have been true at some point. Together they describe several companies wearing the same name badge.

A retrieved answer may choose one version. It may blur them into a vague description such as business software for reporting and project work. You do not get to choose which sentence survives. Research into multi-aspect retrieval describes how [queries that require several semantically distinct documents can be difficult because the relevant material may sit far apart](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05085v5).

Agreement provides a practical way to reduce that uncertainty. If the homepage, pricing page, LinkedIn profile and directory records use the same category, audience and product description, the model has less contradictory material to reconcile. This remains an operating rule rather than a promise about a particular answer. Retrieval can miss the best page, and a language model can still produce a poor summary.

The awkward part is that old positioning does not disappear when you stop saying it in sales calls. It remains on the page where you published it. The product changed, the homepage changed, and the directory profile from launch week kept its original description.

## Audit claims instead of polishing copy

Make a list of the pages most likely to describe the company:

- Your homepage
- Your pricing page
- Your LinkedIn company profile
- Directory and marketplace listings
- Your latest blog posts
- Your About page
- Any help page that explains who the product is for

Put the pages across the top of a spreadsheet. Down the side, write the claims a stranger would need to understand the company. Include the category, audience, product, price, availability, supported locations and named integrations. Leave out brand adjectives. Innovative and intuitive rarely cause a factual contradiction. A different price does.

Copy the exact wording from each page into the relevant cell. Mark every row where the claims differ. Also mark empty cells when the omission could change the meaning. A homepage for finance departments and a LinkedIn profile with no audience at all still leave room for an old directory listing to supply the answer.

Read whole sections rather than isolated sentences. Research on customer-service retrieval found that [splitting structured records into plain text chunks can disconnect related material and leave an answer incomplete](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.17723v1). Your website is a different setting, but the warning travels well. The sentence that names your audience may sit far from the sentence that explains the product, and an extracted passage may capture only one of them.

You are looking for factual disagreement, stale positioning and ambiguous omissions. This is an audit, so resist the temptation to rewrite every sentence while you inspect it. A prettier spreadsheet full of contradictions is still a spreadsheet full of contradictions.

## Fix the pages you can publish yourself

Begin with the pages you control. Update the homepage and pricing page, then the company profile and recent posts that describe the current offer. The order can change when another page receives more attention or contains a more serious error. A false price deserves attention before an unfashionable tagline.

Historical posts need judgement. If an old article records a product that existed at the time, rewriting it can create a new kind of inaccuracy. Add a dated editor’s note and point readers to the current product page. If the post presents stale information as current advice, revise it or remove it from publication.

Next, contact the owners of directory records, marketplace profiles and articles you cannot edit. Send the replacement sentence and the page that confirms it. A precise request gives the owner less work than a message that says the profile feels out of date.

Keep a record of pages that remain wrong. Retrieval systems may draw context from several sources, and [the contextual information returned by retrieval affects the final output](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.13163v2). You may never control the whole set. You can still make the clearest and most current pages agree.

## Agreement cannot create missing relevance

Consistent pages can help an AI answer describe your company accurately. They cannot make your company appear in a category that no available page connects you with.

Suppose Northstar wants to be mentioned when someone asks about forecasting software. Its pages agree that it provides reporting software, while none discusses forecasting. Repeating the reporting description across more profiles does not create evidence for the missing category.

That gap calls for separate work. Publish a page that explains the forecasting use case if the product supports it. Show how a customer uses it. Earn coverage from a publication that already writes about the category. Each claim still needs to be true. Category inclusion built on wishful wording tends to produce a more polished error.

This boundary matters because an audit gives you a free place to start, rather than a complete plan for appearing in every AI answer. Agreement improves the evidence that exists. It does not manufacture relevance, authority or independent coverage.

## Compare the answers after the pages change

Come back on the same date next month. Use the same prompt in a fresh conversation and copy the new answer beneath the old one.

Compare them line by line. Mark stale claims that disappeared, accurate claims that appeared, and vague phrases that remained. Check whether the updated pages now appear in ordinary search results. If the answer stays unchanged, you still will not know the precise cause. The system may have retrieved different material, revisited none of your edits or relied on information outside your audit.

Keep both answers. They give you a repeatable test instead of a memory that ChatGPT seemed vague last time. The next useful edit is the sentence that remains wrong everywhere a stranger can find it.

alibaba/qwen3.7-plus.title: ChatGPT describes your company from five pages, so make them agree
alibaba/qwen3.7-plus.content:
Ask ChatGPT to describe your company today and write down its answer sentence by sentence. You will see a vague line or a description of a competitor. The model builds your description from a handful of web pages. When those pages agree, the description is accurate. When they disagree, the model blurs the facts or picks the wrong one. You need a first thing to do this week that costs no money. Start with the pages the model actually reads.

## A small company gives an AI a handful of pages to read

A [retrieval augmented generation system](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05085v5) fetches documents to ground its answers in verifiable information. For a massive enterprise, the model pulls from thousands of internal wikis, press releases and support tickets. For a small company, the model only finds a few public pages. Your homepage, your pricing page, your LinkedIn profile and a directory listing carry the entire weight of your public identity. Whatever those pages agree on becomes your description. This includes the features you stopped believing last year and the pricing you changed in March. The model reads the text and synthesizes a single truth from the fragments it retrieves. You gave it five pages and it gave you a paragraph. The paragraph is only as good as the five pages.

## Contradictions force the model to guess

When two pages disagree, the answer picks one or blurs both. Your homepage might promise a self-serve onboarding flow while your pricing page lists a mandatory implementation fee. The model sees both claims. It lacks the context to choose. It might tell a prospect that onboarding costs extra. It might tell them onboarding is free. The model decides which version to output based on the semantic weight of the surrounding words. These systems [segment text into fixed-length chunks](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.17723v1) and disconnect related content. The [retrieval process returns the most relevant documents](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.07620v1), and the generator combines them into a final response. When the retrieved chunks contain opposing facts, the generator has to bridge the gap. It uses statistical probability to guess which fact belongs in the final sentence. A contradiction on your site becomes a hallucination in the chat window. The prospect reads the chat and assumes the model knows something you forgot to update on your pricing page. You lose the deal because the model guessed wrong on a fact you control.

## Audit your pages for every differing claim

List the pages the model can read. Put your homepage, pricing page, LinkedIn company page, directory listings and your last few blog posts in a spreadsheet. Mark every claim that differs between them. Look at your product names, your target audience, your pricing tiers and your core features. If your homepage says you serve enterprise teams and your blog says you serve freelancers, you created a contradiction. The model reads both and averages them out. You end up described as serving mid-market teams that never existed. Look at your pricing tiers. If your pricing page lists three tiers but your blog post from last month mentions a fourth tier that you sunsetted, the model will describe a four-tier product. The prospect asks for the fourth tier in the demo. You have to explain that the model read an old blog post. This happens because the model treats all retrieved text as current truth. It lacks a timestamp for your business decisions. Look at your integrations. If your homepage lists Slack and your directory listing lists Microsoft Teams, the model assumes you support both. If you dropped Slack support last quarter, the model still promises it to every prospect. Find every mismatch and write it down.

## Fix the pages you control first

Change the pages you own to match. Rewrite the homepage, update the pricing page and align your LinkedIn profile. This takes an afternoon. Then ask the owners of the directory listings to change theirs. A third-party review site might hold an outdated description of your product. Send them the new text. They might ignore your request today, but you removed the contradiction from your own domain. The model weights your own domain higher than a random directory. When the model fetches pages, it trusts the primary source over the aggregator. Fix your own house first. The directory listings will eventually catch up, or the model will stop weighting them as heavily once your primary domain is consistent.

## Agreeing pages make the description accurate and leave category rankings alone

If no tech blog has called you a project management tool, the model leaves you out of that category entirely. You have to write the category into existence on pages the model can read. Writing the category into existence means publishing content that explicitly links your product to the category name. A blog post titled 'How to use our tool for project management' gives the model the exact phrase it needs. Without that phrase on a page the model can read, no amount of internal agreement will put you in the project management category. The model needs the explicit text to make the connection. Agreement fixes the details of your description. It leaves the category boundaries exactly as they were. A founder might fix five pages and expect the model to suddenly recommend them over a competitor with fifty published articles. That is a different problem. Fixing contradictions stops the model from lying about your current product. You fixed the truth and left the fame to the marketing team.

## Ask again in a month and compare the answers

Wait a month for the search index to update. Ask ChatGPT the exact same question. Write down the new answer sentence by sentence. Compare the two answers line by line. The vague line should now contain your specific product names. The wrong pricing should match your current tiers. A competitor name should disappear from your description. You spent an afternoon fixing text on a few pages. The model now tells the truth about your company.
